title: Generative AI in K-12 Education: The CyberScholar Initiative
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether CyberScholar, a generative AI writing assistant, can support K-12 students’ writing through formative feedback aligned to classroom rubrics and materials. The central question is how a GenAI tool can be used for writing support in authentic school contexts, and whether its feedback is perceived as useful by students and teachers.

The intervention was piloted in four public schools in the United States across middle and high school grades, with writing tasks in English Language Arts, Social Studies, and Modern World History. CyberScholar was customized using teachers’ prompts, rubrics, books, and slides through retrieval-augmented generation and prompt engineering. The study involved 121 students and 4 teachers, with data gathered through observations, surveys, and interviews over an implementation period from August 2024 to January 2025.

Using an exploratory multiple case study and thematic qualitative analysis, the authors found that students valued the tool’s detailed feedback, interactivity, perceived improvements in writing quality, and rubric-based scoring. Teachers were positioned less as sole evaluators and more as managers of AI-supported feedback loops. The paper concludes that GenAI can complement teacher feedback in K-12 writing instruction when it is contextually aligned, interactive, and pedagogically grounded, though it should not replace teachers.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI writing assistant/chatbot used to generate formative feedback on student writing and support revision in K-12 settings.
identified_tools.use_case: Piloted as CyberScholar, a GenAI assistant customized with teachers’ rubrics, instructional materials, and expectations to provide formative feedback on student writing across grades 7, 8, 10, and 11 in four U.S. schools.

findings.finding_summary: In this qualitative multiple-case study, 121 K-12 students used CyberScholar for writing revisions across English Language Arts, Social Studies, and Modern World History. Students reported that the tool supported writing development through detailed and specific feedback, interactive clarification, perceived improvements in writing quality, and ratings aligned with rubric criteria; 36 students said they would use it again, while 11 were hesitant.
findings.measure: Student post-survey comments, interviews, and classroom observations of perceived usefulness for writing support
findings.sample_size: n=121 students; n=4 teachers; post-survey n=54; interviews n=8 students and 1 teacher

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports subgroup and setting variation descriptively rather than with statistical tests. Interactive follow-up questioning was available only in Schools C and D, and student comments varied by school/context; the authors also note that the tool was customized to different rubrics, subject areas, and school settings, but no comparative effect sizes were reported by grade band, subject, teacher experience, or school context.
findings.measure: Descriptive qualitative differences across schools, grades, and subjects

quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative multiple-case study with surveys, interviews, and observations rather than an experimental design. It provides contextual evidence of use, but there are no causal estimates or statistical tests.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive perceived usefulness and practical alignment with teacher rubrics, but no effect sizes are available. Impact appears promising yet uncertain because outcomes are based on participant perceptions and descriptive evidence.
